children: Brazil's 2027 budget bill projects the country's first effective primary surplus since 2022, highlighting the government's confidence that fiscal accounts are on the mend despite market expectations for continued deficits and rising public debt.

The budget bill, submitted to Congress on Monday, estimated an effective primary surplus of 18.6 billion reais ($3.59 billion) for the central government, equivalent to 0.13% of gross domestic product.
If achieved, it would mark the first annual primary surplus for the central government since 2022, when the surplus amounted to 0.55% of GDP.

The government's projections are considerably more optimistic than market forecasts, underscoring the gap between Brasilia's expectations for fiscal consolidation and investor skepticism over debt stabilization amid the rapid growth of mandatory spending and a hefty interest bill.
Economists surveyed weekly by the central bank expect Brazil to post a primary deficit of 0.4% of GDP in 2027 and do not see Latin America's largest economy returning to balanced accounts until 2030.
Brazil's fiscal target for next year is a primary surplus of 0.5% of GDP, with a tolerance band of 0.25 percentage point in either direction.
Under the fiscal framework, however, the government is allowed to exclude certain expenditures when assessing compliance with the target, most notably part of its stock of court-ordered payments.
On that adjusted basis, the government projects a primary surplus of 83.4 billion reais, equivalent to 0.56% of GDP, in 2027.
During President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's current term, the central government's effective primary balance, as measured by the central bank, has remained in deficit.
The shortfall stood at 2.42% of GDP in 2023, narrowed to 0.39% in 2024 and widened slightly to 0.46% in 2025. The government is forecasting a deficit of 0.4% of GDP this year.
The 2027 budget proposal also assumes economic growth of 2.46% and inflation of 3.6% next year.
